title: ABG: acid–base reading

findings.where: src/diagrams/abg.jsx — compensationLimit() respiratory-acidosis branch, INTERPRETED bounds, and courseText(); affects generated worked examples
findings.title: Severe hypercapnia can produce a falsely reassuring acute-compensation fit
findings.problem: For pH 7.13, PaCO₂ 140, HCO₃⁻ 45, the values agree mathematically and pass the supported bounds. The interpreter calculates an acute HCO₃⁻ band of 34–44 ± 2, accepts 45, and says it fits a PaCO₂ change of hours. This extrapolates the upper coefficient far beyond its useful bedside range. Acute nonrenal buffering generally raises bicarbonate only modestly—commonly described as rarely exceeding approximately 30–32 mEq/L. A bicarbonate of 45 requires consideration of pre-existing renal compensation or an added metabolic alkalosis, not an uncomplicated acute-buffering explanation. The history caveat does not correct the displayed acute estimate.
findings.fix: Define reference-validated applicability limits for the respiratory compensation rules. Outside those limits, withhold the acute/chronic fit rather than extending the linear equation across the entire PaCO₂ 10–150 range. Explain that marked bicarbonate elevation may reflect chronic compensation, an acute-on-chronic disorder, or a metabolic component. Add regression cases for severe hypercapnia, including 7.13/140/45.

assessment: The pictured example is coherent. The unrestricted interpreter still has a clinical problem: it extrapolates acute respiratory-acidosis compensation into severe hypercapnia beyond the reliable range of the bedside rule.
